Grapegatherers
grāp'gath-er-ers
n. pl. (those who harvest a vineyard; in the prophets, a figure for a judgment that nevertheless leaves gleanings, unlike a thief)
A compound of grape (Old French grape, a bunch) and gatherer, rendering Hebrew botsrim, from batsar, to cut off or gather grapes — the vintagers.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs in two oracles that share a single argument. Jeremiah, against Edom: “If grapegatherers come to thee, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough” (Jeremiah 49:9). Obadiah, against the same nation: “If thieves came to thee, if robbers by night, (how art thou cut off!) would they not have stolen till they had enough? if the grapegatherers came to thee, would they not leave some grapes?” (Obadiah 1:5). The reasoning runs by contrast. A vintager works under the law that forbids stripping a vineyard bare, so something is always left for the poor and the stranger; a thief takes only what he wants and leaves the rest. Either way, something remains. What is coming on Edom will be worse than both: “But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself” (Jeremiah 49:10). Nothing left at all. Micah uses the same picture for his own grief at a nation with no righteous man in it: “Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat” (Micah 7:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a gatherer as one who collects, and vintage as the produce of the vine for the year, the time of gathering grapes.

expand to see more

GATHERER, n. One who gathers or collects.

VINTAGE, n. The produce of the vine for the season, in grapes or in wine.

2. The time of gathering the crop of grapes.

GLEAN, v.t. To gather the stalks and ears of grain which reapers leave behind them.

VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 49:9 — "If grapegatherers come to thee, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough."

Obadiah 1:5 — "If thieves came to thee, if robbers by night, (how art thou cut off!) would they not have stolen till they had enough? if the grapegatherers came to thee, would they not leave some grapes?"

Jeremiah 49:10 — "But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself: his seed is spoiled, and his brethren, and his neighbours, and he is not."

Micah 7:1 — "Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit."

Modern Corruption

The gleaning law behind the figure is read as an antique charity provision, when it is a limit God imposed on the rights of an owner over his own field.

expand to see more

The whole force of Jeremiah 49:9 depends on a law the modern reader has to be told about. Leviticus 19:10 forbids gleaning a vineyard bare or gathering the fallen grapes; they are to be left for the poor and the stranger. That is why a vintager is a lower bar than a thief in the prophet's argument: even a legitimate harvester is under a restriction. The law asserts something the current debate over property rarely allows to be said — that ownership is real and is not absolute, because the owner is himself a tenant under God. Neither of the standard modern positions holds that: one treats property as absolute, the other abolishes it. Scripture does neither, and leaves the corners of the field standing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word. The principle to recover is the dignity of the arrangement. The gleaning law does not transfer the harvest; it leaves it in the field, so that the poor gather it with their own hands and are fed by work rather than by handout. Ruth is the extended illustration, and Boaz's charge to his young men to let fall some handfuls of purpose is the law kept generously. That pattern — provision the poor must still labour to take up, arranged so that no one is humiliated in receiving it — is a wiser design than most of what has replaced it, and it came from the same statute book that told the vintager to leave some grapes.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew botsrim, grape-gatherers — Jeremiah 49:9, Obadiah 5; from batsar, to cut off or gather grapes; oleloth, gleaning grapes — Jeremiah 49:9, Micah 7:1.

expand to see more

Hebrew batsar — to cut off, to gather grapes; the root of botsrim, the vintagers.

Hebrew oleloth — the gleanings of a vineyard, what the vintager must leave; Jeremiah 49:9, Micah 7:1, Isaiah 17:6.

Hebrew Esau and Edom — the nation both oracles address, kin to Israel and hostile to her.

Leviticus 19:10 is the law the figure presupposes: thou shalt not glean thy vineyard, neither shalt thou gather every grape.

Ruth 2:16 shows the law kept with generosity: let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her.

Usage

"“Would they not leave some gleaning grapes?” — even the harvester is under a limit."

"“I have made Esau bare” — less left than a thief would leave."

"The corners of the field were never the owner's to take."
